items.stem:
Every senior partner at the firm has argued at least one case before the state supreme court. Maria is a senior partner at the firm. Therefore, Maria has argued at least one case before the state supreme court.

The argument above is most similar in its reasoning to which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All birds have feathers. A penguin is a bird. So a penguin has feathers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most lawyers own at least one suit. Therefore, the lawyer next door owns a suit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anyone who passed the bar studied. Tom studied, so Tom passed the bar.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If it rains, the picnic is canceled. The picnic was canceled, so it rained.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No senator is under 30. Lin is 28, so Lin might be a senator.

items.explanation: The original is a valid universal-instantiation argument: 'All P are Q; x is P; therefore x is Q.' Choice A has identical form. B uses 'most' (probabilistic). C affirms the consequent. D denies the antecedent reversed. E contradicts a universal.

items.stem:
City planner: Building a light-rail line will reduce traffic congestion downtown, because every comparable city that built one saw congestion fall within five years.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the planner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The light-rail line will be more expensive than the planner estimates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some downtown residents oppose the construction noise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Light-rail riders in those cities reported high satisfaction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The comparable cities all simultaneously enacted downtown congestion-pricing tolls.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The proposed line will run mostly underground.

items.explanation: The argument infers causation from correlation across comparable cities. D introduces a confound — congestion-pricing tolls — that may explain the congestion drop instead of the rail line, undermining the causal inference. A attacks cost (irrelevant to congestion). B, C, and E are off-point.

items.stem:
If the contract is enforceable, then it was signed by both parties. The contract was not signed by both parties.

Which one of the following can be properly concluded?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contract is enforceable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The contract is not enforceable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The contract is partially enforceable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only one party intended to be bound.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nothing can be concluded about enforceability.

items.explanation: Modus tollens: 'If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.' If enforceable required both signatures and we lack both signatures, the contract is not enforceable. The other options either affirm the consequent, add facts not given, or reject a valid inference.

items.stem:
Editor: Our new policy requires every opinion piece to cite at least three primary sources. Critics claim this will reduce the diversity of viewpoints we publish, since fewer freelance writers have access to primary sources. But our submission rate has not dropped since the policy took effect, so the critics are mistaken.

The editor's reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it…

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a necessary condition as if it were sufficient.

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes without warrant that all freelance writers lack primary sources.

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider that some published pieces cite more than three sources.

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers a general rule from a single anecdote.

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses the volume of submissions with the diversity of viewpoints in those submissions.

items.explanation: The critics' claim is about *diversity of viewpoints*. The editor rebuts using *submission volume*. Equating the two is the flaw — submission count and viewpoint diversity are different measures, so E names it. A, B, C, and D mischaracterize the structure.

items.stem:
Studies show that people who eat breakfast perform better on cognitive tests in the morning than people who skip breakfast. Therefore, eating breakfast causes improved cognitive performance.

The argument's reasoning is flawed because it…

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on studies that may not be representative.

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to specify what counts as breakfast.

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers causation from correlation without ruling out alternative explanations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes that all cognitive tests measure the same ability.

choices.label: E
choices.text: ignores that some people perform well without breakfast.

items.explanation: Classic correlation ≠ causation flaw. People who eat breakfast may also sleep more, exercise, or have less stress — any of which could be the real cause. The argument fails to rule out these confounders. A, B, D, E are peripheral.

items.stem:
Columnist: Supporters of the new zoning ordinance say it will preserve the neighborhood's historic character. But the supporters have not produced any architectural surveys to back up that claim. So the ordinance will not preserve the historic character.

The columnist's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it…

choices.label: A
choices.text: presupposes what it sets out to prove.

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on a sample that is too small.

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about an individual from claims about a group.

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats absence of evidence as evidence of absence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: appeals to popular opinion rather than to facts.

items.explanation: Lack of supporting evidence does not establish the opposite conclusion (the ordinance might still preserve the character even if no survey has been produced). This appeal-to-ignorance flaw is captured by D. A, B, C, and E describe errors the columnist did not commit.

items.stem:
Lawyer: To win the appeal, the defendant must show either that the trial court misapplied the statute or that the jury was improperly instructed. The trial court did not misapply the statute. So if the defendant wins the appeal, then the jury was improperly instructed.

The lawyer's reasoning depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There are no other grounds on which the appeal could be won.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The defendant will win the appeal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Showing improper jury instructions is sufficient to win an appeal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The jury was in fact improperly instructed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Misapplication of the statute would have been the stronger ground.

items.explanation: The argument lists two ways to win and rules one out, then concludes the other must be the route to a win. That move only works if those two were the *only* possible grounds. Choice A makes that necessary assumption explicit. B, C, D, and E add facts the argument neither states nor requires.

items.stem:
Researcher: Patients who received the new therapy recovered faster than those who received the standard treatment. So the new therapy must be more effective than the standard treatment.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The new therapy is more expensive than the standard treatment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some patients given the standard treatment also recovered quickly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The two groups of patients were similar in age, overall health, and severity of illness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The researcher has studied the standard treatment for many years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A few patients given the new therapy reported mild side effects.

items.explanation: Moving from 'recovered faster' to 'more effective' assumes the two groups were comparable to begin with. C rules out the alternative that the new-therapy group was simply healthier, strengthening the causal claim. A and E raise cost and side-effects, which are irrelevant to effectiveness. B and D neither support nor close the gap.

items.stem:
Only employees who completed the safety course may operate the forklift. No temporary worker has completed the safety course.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some temporary workers may operate the forklift.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every employee who completed the safety course operates the forklift.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anyone who operates the forklift is a temporary worker.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Completing the safety course is sufficient to be allowed to operate the forklift.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No temporary worker may operate the forklift.

items.explanation: 'Only those who completed the course may operate' means operating requires completion (operate → completed). The contrapositive is ¬completed → ¬operate. Since no temporary worker completed the course, no temporary worker may operate the forklift — E. A contradicts this. B and D treat a necessary condition as if it were sufficient. C reverses the conditional.

items.stem:
Critic: If a film is a commercial success, it will be widely imitated. This year's top-grossing comedy has already spawned a dozen imitators. So it was a commercial success.

The critic's reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it…

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes a condition that guarantees an outcome to be required for that outcome.

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a result that the premise says would follow from success as if it established success.

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on a sample of films that is too small to support a generalization.

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes that what is true of one comedy is true of all comedies.

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses the popularity of a film with its artistic merit.

items.explanation: The premise says success → imitation. The critic observes imitation and infers success, affirming the consequent — imitation could arise for other reasons. B names this error. A describes the converse mistake (necessary vs. sufficient) the critic did not make. C, D, and E raise issues the argument does not turn on.

items.stem:
Anyone who understands the proof will pass the exam. Therefore, Dana will pass the exam.

The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dana understands the proof.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dana has studied harder than anyone else in the class.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Everyone who passes the exam understands the proof.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most students who understand the proof pass the exam.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Anyone who passes the exam will later understand the proof.

items.explanation: This is a sufficient-assumption question: find the premise that, added to 'understands the proof → passes the exam,' guarantees the conclusion that Dana passes. Only A does it — if Dana understands the proof, the rule forces the conclusion that Dana passes. B is irrelevant (studying is not the stated trigger). D is merely probabilistic ('most'), so it cannot guarantee the result. C and E reverse the conditional (pass → understand), which never licenses concluding that Dana passes.

items.stem:
If the witness is credible, then the alibi holds. If the alibi holds, then the defendant was not at the scene. The witness is credible.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The defendant was not at the scene.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The alibi does not hold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The witness is not credible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the defendant was not at the scene, then the witness is credible.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The defendant was at the scene.

items.explanation: Chain the conditionals — credible → alibi holds → not at scene — and apply modus ponens to the given fact that the witness is credible. The conclusion that follows is that the defendant was not at the scene (A). B and C contradict the premises. D reverses a conditional (affirming the consequent) and is not guaranteed. E directly contradicts the valid conclusion.

items.stem:
If a witness is impeached with a prior inconsistent statement, then the witness's credibility is called into question. Officer Reyes was impeached with a prior inconsistent statement during cross-examination.

Which one of the following can be properly concluded on the basis of the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Officer Reyes's testimony will be excluded from evidence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Officer Reyes's credibility has been called into question.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any witness whose credibility is called into question has been impeached with a prior inconsistent statement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A witness who is not impeached with a prior inconsistent statement will not have his credibility called into question.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It cannot be determined whether Officer Reyes's credibility has been called into question.

items.explanation: B follows by modus ponens: the conditional's antecedent (impeachment with a prior inconsistent statement) is satisfied by Officer Reyes, so the stated consequent (credibility called into question) must hold. A introduces exclusion of testimony, a consequence the stimulus never mentions, so it is out of scope. C commits the converse, wrongly assuming impeachment by prior inconsistent statement is the only way credibility could be questioned. D commits the inverse, wrongly inferring that failing to satisfy the antecedent guarantees the consequent fails too. E wrongly denies that a determinate conclusion is available, when modus ponens settles the matter with certainty.

items.stem:
If an appellate brief exceeds the court's page limit, then the clerk will reject the filing. The defendant's appellate brief exceeds the court's page limit.

Which one of the following can be properly concluded on the basis of the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any brief that the clerk rejects must exceed the court's page limit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A brief that does not exceed the court's page limit will not be rejected by the clerk.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It cannot be determined whether the clerk will reject the defendant's brief.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The clerk will reject the defendant's brief.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The defendant's brief also fails to comply with the court's formatting requirements.

items.explanation: D follows by modus ponens: exceeding the page limit is sufficient to trigger rejection, and the defendant's brief satisfies that antecedent, so rejection must follow. A commits the converse, treating rejection as proof that a brief exceeded the limit, when the stimulus never states that exceeding the limit is the only route to rejection. B commits the inverse, wrongly assuming that not triggering the rule guarantees the opposite outcome. C wrongly denies that a valid inference is available, when modus ponens settles it. E introduces an unstated defect (formatting) the stimulus never mentions, so it is out of scope.

items.stem:
If a title company fails to record a deed within thirty days of closing, then the buyer's claim to the property loses priority over later recorded claims. The title company handling Ms. Alvarez's purchase failed to record her deed within thirty days of closing.

Which one of the following can be properly concluded on the basis of the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ms. Alvarez's claim to the property loses priority over later recorded claims.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any buyer whose claim loses priority had a title company that failed to record the deed within thirty days.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A buyer whose deed is recorded within thirty days will never lose priority to a later recorded claim.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether Ms. Alvarez's claim loses priority cannot be determined from the information given.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ms. Alvarez is entitled to sue the title company for damages.

items.explanation: A is the direct modus ponens conclusion: the rule's trigger (failure to record within thirty days) is satisfied, so the stated consequence (loss of priority) must follow. B commits the converse, assuming late recording is the only route to losing priority. C commits the inverse, wrongly assuming that satisfying a different condition (timely recording) guarantees the opposite outcome, something the stimulus never claims. D wrongly treats the conclusion as indeterminate when modus ponens makes it certain. E introduces a remedy (a damages suit) never discussed in the stimulus, so it is out of scope.

items.stem:
If an employee discloses a trade secret to a competitor, then the employee breaches the confidentiality agreement. Deshawn, an employee at Havelock Robotics, disclosed a trade secret to a competitor.

Which one of the following can be properly concluded on the basis of the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any employee who breaches the confidentiality agreement has disclosed a trade secret to a competitor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An employee who does not disclose a trade secret to a competitor will not breach the confidentiality agreement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether Deshawn breached the confidentiality agreement cannot be determined from the information given.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deshawn will likely be terminated from his position at Havelock Robotics.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deshawn breached the confidentiality agreement.

items.explanation: E follows by modus ponens: disclosing a trade secret to a competitor is sufficient to trigger a breach, and Deshawn did exactly that, so the breach must follow. A commits the converse, assuming disclosure to a competitor is the only way to breach the agreement. B commits the inverse, wrongly inferring that not disclosing to a competitor guarantees no breach. C wrongly denies that the conclusion can be determined, when modus ponens settles it with certainty. D introduces an unstated consequence (termination) that the stimulus never addresses, making it out of scope.

items.stem:
If a document is to be admitted as a valid affidavit, then it must be signed in the presence of a notary. This document was not signed in the presence of a notary.

Which one of the following can be properly concluded from the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The document was signed in the presence of a witness who is not a notary.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The document cannot be admitted as a valid affidavit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The document was admitted as a valid affidavit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a document is signed in the presence of a notary, then it may be admitted as a valid affidavit.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No conclusion can be drawn about whether the document is a valid affidavit.

items.explanation: The rule given is 'if a document is to be admitted as a valid affidavit (P), it must be signed before a notary (Q),' paired with the negated consequent: this document was not signed before a notary (not-Q). Modus tollens licenses the negated antecedent: the document cannot be admitted as a valid affidavit, choice B. A introduces a fact never supplied by the stimulus — whether any other witness was present is simply unknown. C asserts P, the exact opposite of the guaranteed conclusion; the negated consequent rules P out rather than supporting it. D states the converse of the original rule, swapping which condition is sufficient and which is necessary; nothing in the stimulus establishes that being notarized is sufficient for admissibility. E wrongly claims no conclusion is available, but modus tollens makes B a certain, valid inference from the two given statements.

items.stem:
If a notice of appeal is filed on time, then the appellate court will have jurisdiction to hear the case. The appellate court does not have jurisdiction to hear this case.

Which one of the following can be properly concluded from the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The appellate court has jurisdiction to hear the case.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The notice of appeal was filed on time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the appellate court has jurisdiction to hear a case, then the notice of appeal in that case was filed on time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The notice of appeal was not filed on time.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether the notice of appeal was filed on time cannot be determined from the statements above.

items.explanation: The rule given is 'if filed on time (P), then the court has jurisdiction (Q),' and we're told the court lacks jurisdiction (not-Q). Modus tollens converts this negated consequent into the negated antecedent: the notice was not filed on time, choice D. A asserts Q — that the court has jurisdiction — which directly contradicts the stimulus's second sentence. B asserts P, the reverse of the valid conclusion; the negated consequent rules P out rather than supporting it. C states the converse of the original rule, treating jurisdiction as though it guarantees timely filing; the stimulus never licenses that reversed relationship. E incorrectly denies that any conclusion can be drawn, but the negated consequent guarantees D by modus tollens.

items.stem:
No conclusive study has ever shown that the herbal supplement Vitalex causes liver damage. Therefore, Vitalex is safe for long-term use.

The argument's reasoning is questionable because it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on the personal testimony of Vitalex users rather than controlled data.

choices.label: B
choices.text: attacks the credibility of scientists who have criticized Vitalex.

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to specify what would count as "long-term use."

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the absence of proof that Vitalex is harmful as proof that it is safe.

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws its conclusion from a study population that may be too small to detect rare side effects.

items.explanation: The argument moves directly from 'no study has proven Vitalex causes harm' to 'Vitalex is safe,' which is the appeal-to-ignorance flaw named in D: absence of proof of harm is not proof of safety -- it may simply mean the right study hasn't been done yet. A is wrong because the argument never mentions user testimony; it cites the absence of studies, not personal accounts. B is wrong because the argument never disputes anyone's credibility -- it doesn't engage with critics at all. C is a red herring: the term 'long-term use' is not what makes the inference weak; the inference fails regardless of how that phrase is defined. E misdescribes the argument, which rests on the total absence of confirming studies, not on a specific study's sample size -- no such study is discussed. D alone captures the actual gap between the premise and the conclusion.

items.stem:
Auditors found no documentation proving that Meridian Consulting overbilled its clients last year. City officials therefore concluded that Meridian did not overbill its clients.

The city officials' reasoning is flawed because it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats the absence of documentation proving overbilling as proof that no overbilling occurred.

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes that all consulting firms behave the same way when it comes to billing practices.

choices.label: C
choices.text: questions the auditors' competence rather than addressing the substance of their findings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to define what conduct would count as "overbilling."

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on a single year's audit to draw a conclusion about the firm's overall practices.

items.explanation: The officials infer 'no overbilling occurred' solely from 'no documentation proves it occurred' -- but missing proof of overbilling is not proof of its absence; the documentation might simply not exist or might not have been found. A states this precisely. B is wrong because the argument makes no claim about consulting firms generally -- it is confined to Meridian. C is wrong because the argument never disputes the auditors' competence; it accepts their findings and misinterprets what those findings show. D is a red herring: however 'overbilling' is defined, the inference from 'no proof found' to 'none occurred' is equally unsupported. E is wrong because the argument's flaw is not about how much data was examined but about what conclusion an absence of evidence licenses; the single-year scope is not what makes the inference fail. Only A identifies the actual gap.

items.stem:
In Rivertown, every building permit application is reviewed by the planning board. Any application reviewed by the planning board that proposes a structure taller than 40 feet is also referred to the historic commission. The application for the Elm Street project proposes a structure that is 55 feet tall.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Elm Street application will be referred to the historic commission.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Elm Street application will be approved by the historic commission.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only applications proposing structures taller than 40 feet are referred to the historic commission.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the Elm Street project's height is reduced to 35 feet, the application will not be referred to the historic commission.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The planning board reviewed the Elm Street application before its height reached 55 feet.

items.explanation: A is correct: every application is reviewed by the planning board (so Elm Street's is), and any reviewed application proposing a structure over 40 feet is referred to the historic commission; since Elm Street proposes 55 feet, referral follows from two applications of the given rules. B claims approval, but referral to a body is not the same as approval by it -- a scope shift beyond what is stated. C illegitimately converts the sufficient condition (over 40 feet triggers referral) into a necessary one, asserting no other route to referral could exist -- unsupported. D reasons from an unaddressed hypothetical height change and wrongly assumes the 40-foot threshold is the only possible trigger; this denies the antecedent invalidly. E introduces an unsupported temporal detail about timing that the stimulus never discusses.

items.stem: Although rising interest rates have slowed home sales nationwide, the downtown condominium market here should be classified as healthy rather than declining. Sales data show that condominiums priced below $400,000 continue to sell within two weeks of listing, since first-time buyers view them as an affordable alternative to renting. Furthermore, developers are still breaking ground on three new condo towers this year, a sign of confidence that would make little sense in a genuinely declining market.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rising interest rates have slowed home sales nationwide.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The downtown condominium market here should be regarded as healthy, not declining.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Condominiums priced below $400,000 sell within two weeks of being listed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: First-time buyers view condominiums under $400,000 as an affordable alternative to renting.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Developers would not break ground on new towers in a market that is genuinely declining.

items.explanation: The conclusion, tucked into the sentence right after the concession, is that the downtown condo market should be seen as healthy rather than declining -- everything else in the stimulus supports that claim, so B restates it correctly. A merely restates the concession about interest rates, which the author grants before pivoting to disagree; it is the point conceded, not the point argued. C reports the fast-selling-condo data, a premise offered as evidence, not the claim being defended. D gives the reason (via 'since') for why cheaper condos sell quickly -- a premise one level further down, easy to mistake for the point because of its confident, explanatory phrasing. E restates the developer-confidence premise, which supports the conclusion but is not itself what the argument sets out to establish.

items.stem:
Historians have never found any document proving that the ancient city of Kallira lacked a functioning irrigation system. Therefore, Kallira must have had a functioning irrigation system.

The historians' reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: assumes that every ancient city needed an irrigation system to survive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on the testimony of historians who may be biased toward a particular theory of Kallira's history.

choices.label: C
choices.text: concludes that a claim is true merely because no evidence has been found to refute it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to define what would count as a "functioning" irrigation system.

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizes from the practices of one ancient city to ancient cities generally.

items.explanation: The argument's only support for 'Kallira had irrigation' is that no document disproves it -- but a missing disproof is not proof of truth; the relevant records may simply be lost or never written. That is exactly the error C names. A is wrong because the argument never claims irrigation was necessary for survival -- it just asserts Kallira had one. B mischaracterizes the argument: no historian's testimony or bias is invoked, only the absence of a document. D is a red herring -- however 'functioning' is defined, the inference from 'no disproof' to 'true' remains equally weak. E is wrong because the argument draws no conclusion about other ancient cities at all; it stays narrowly focused on Kallira. Only C identifies the genuine gap between premise and conclusion.

items.stem:
Since no employee has ever filed a formal complaint about the safety of the new assembly-line robots, the robots must pose no safety risk to workers.

The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: questions the motives of employees who might raise safety concerns.

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes that employees would report a real safety risk if one existed, rather than establishing that no risk exists.

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on too short an operating history to rule out rare mechanical failures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to specify what would count as a "safety risk."

choices.label: E
choices.text: compares the robots to a different, unrelated type of machinery.

items.explanation: The argument treats the absence of complaints as if it settles the question of danger, but silence could mean many things besides safety -- workers may not notice a risk, may fear retaliation, or may not know how to file a complaint. B names this: the argument merely assumes complaints would occur if risk existed, rather than showing risk is actually absent. A is wrong because the argument never questions any employee's motives -- it simply notes an absence of complaints. C is a sample-size-style distractor that doesn't apply here: the argument's flaw is treating silence as proof, not relying on a short observation window, which is not mentioned. D is a red herring -- no matter how 'safety risk' is defined, the leap from 'no complaints' to 'no risk' remains unjustified. E is wrong because the argument makes no comparison to any other machinery. B alone captures the appeal-to-ignorance gap.

items.stem: Principle: A retailer may decline to complete a sale at an item's posted price only if (1) the posted price is so far below the item's evident value that no reasonable shopper could believe it reflects the retailer's intended price, and (2) the retailer informs the shopper of the pricing error before the sale is finalized. Which of the following situations conforms to this principle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A jewelry store had priced a diamond ring at $19.99 instead of $1,999.00. A customer purchased the ring and the sale was completed; only afterward did the store call the customer to explain the labeling error and ask that the ring be returned.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A furniture store had priced a leather sofa at $45 instead of $4,500 because of a decimal-point error. Before ringing up the sale, the cashier told the customer about the error and declined to sell the sofa for $45.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A bookstore priced a novel at $8, well below its usual $25, as part of an intentional clearance sale. Midway through the transaction, the manager decided she would rather not sell it that cheaply and told the customer before completing the sale.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An electronics store had priced a laptop at $4 instead of $400 because of a scanner glitch. The clerk noticed the obvious error, canceled the transaction without explanation, and said nothing to the confused customer about why.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A grocery store had correctly priced milk at $3.79. A new cashier mistakenly believed this was a pricing error and, before completing the sale, told the customer she would not honor what she wrongly took to be a mispriced item.

items.explanation: The principle requires BOTH that the price be so obviously wrong no reasonable shopper could think it intended, AND that the retailer notify the shopper before the sale is finalized. B satisfies both: the $45 sofa price is an obvious decimal error, and the cashier disclosed it and declined before completing the sale -- this is the credited answer. A meets condition (1) but violates condition (2)'s timing: notice came after the sale was completed, not before. C fails condition (1): an intentional clearance markdown is not an obvious pricing error, so the retailer had no principle-based license to back out. D meets condition (1) but fails condition (2): the store never informed the customer of the error at all. E fails condition (1): the milk was priced correctly, so there was no error to invoke, regardless that notice was given before the sale.

items.stem:
If a shipment passes customs inspection, it is released to the distributor. Every shipment either passes customs inspection or fails it. Any shipment that fails customs inspection is flagged for a compliance review. The shipment from Pier 12 was not released to the distributor.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The shipment from Pier 12 passed customs inspection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every shipment that is flagged for compliance review failed customs inspection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The shipment from Pier 12 was flagged for compliance review.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The shipment from Pier 12 will eventually be released to the distributor.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only shipments from Pier 12 are flagged for compliance review.

items.explanation: C is correct. Since the shipment was not released, the contrapositive of the first rule shows it did not pass inspection; because every shipment either passes or fails, it therefore failed, and the third rule then requires that it be flagged for compliance review. A directly contradicts this modus tollens result. B converts the one-directional rule 'fails, therefore flagged' into its converse 'flagged, therefore failed,' and further overgeneralizes it to every shipment ever flagged. D asserts an eventual release that nothing in the stimulus supports -- the shipment has already been established as not released, and no timeline is given. E takes a fact about one shipment and unjustifiably restricts flagging to shipments from that single pier.

items.stem:
If a manuscript is accepted for publication, it has passed peer review. Any manuscript that has passed peer review does not contain plagiarized material. It has been confirmed that the manuscript submitted by Chen contains plagiarized material.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chen's manuscript passed peer review.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every manuscript that contains plagiarized material is rejected outright.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If Chen's manuscript had not contained plagiarized material, it would have been accepted for publication.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The plagiarized material in Chen's manuscript was discovered during peer review.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chen's manuscript was not accepted for publication.

items.explanation: E is correct. The second rule's contrapositive shows that any manuscript containing plagiarized material has not passed peer review; the first rule's contrapositive then shows that any manuscript that has not passed peer review was not accepted for publication. Chaining these through Chen's manuscript yields that it was not accepted. A directly contradicts this chain. B overgeneralizes from Chen's single manuscript to a universal claim about all manuscripts, and asserts an outcome ('rejected outright') never mentioned in the stimulus. C mistakes the absence of plagiarism for a sufficient condition for acceptance, when the stimulus only makes passing peer review necessary for acceptance. D introduces an unsupported claim about when and how the plagiarism was discovered.

items.stem: Some parents argue that youth chess leagues are not worth the cost because few participants become professional players. Still, local youth chess leagues deserve continued funding, since players consistently show measurable gains in concentration and planning skills that carry over into schoolwork. These cognitive gains, moreover, tend to persist for years after a child stops playing competitively, since the strategic habits chess builds become part of how a child approaches any complex problem.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Few participants in youth chess leagues go on to become professional players.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Youth chess players show measurable gains in concentration and planning skills that carry over into schoolwork.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cognitive gains from playing youth chess tend to persist for years after a child stops competing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Local youth chess leagues deserve continued funding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The strategic habits chess builds become part of how a child approaches any complex problem.

items.explanation: The author concedes that few players turn pro but pivots with 'Still' to argue that funding should continue -- that claim, D, is the main conclusion, and everything after it is evidence for it. A merely repeats the conceded point used to open the opposing view, not the author's own claim. B cites the concentration-and-planning-skills data, the first piece of support, introduced by 'since' -- a premise, not the point being proved. C reports a second premise, that the gains persist for years, again offered as evidence for continued funding rather than as the funding claim itself. E goes one level deeper still, explaining why the gains persist; it supports C, which in turn supports D, making it a premise twice removed from the conclusion.

items.stem: Some managers concede that fully remote employees report higher job satisfaction than their in-office peers. Nevertheless, the firm should not extend its remote-work pilot program to additional departments, because departments that shifted to remote work last year saw a measurable decline in cross-team collaboration, and because that decline in collaboration preceded a slowdown in the firm's product-development timeline. A firm that cannot ship products on schedule risks losing customers to faster-moving competitors.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fully remote employees report higher job satisfaction than employees who work in the office.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Departments that shifted to remote work last year experienced a decline in cross-team collaboration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The firm should not extend its remote-work pilot program to additional departments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The decline in cross-team collaboration among remote departments preceded a slowdown in the firm's product-development timeline.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A firm that cannot ship products on schedule risks losing customers to faster-moving competitors.

items.explanation: The conclusion is the recommendation against expanding the pilot program, C, introduced right after the concession and supported by everything that follows. A merely restates the point the author grants to remote-work advocates before arguing against expansion -- it is the concession, not the claim. B and D report the two 'because'-marked premises about the collaboration decline and its timing relative to the product slowdown; both are evidence, not the point being argued. E sits last in the stimulus and states a general risk about missed schedules, which is easy to mistake for the payoff simply because it comes at the end -- but it is a further premise explaining why the collaboration decline matters, not the author's main claim.

items.stem:
A gym chain reports that members who use its mobile app to log workouts lose more weight, on average, than members who do not use the app. The gym's marketing director concludes that using the app causes weight loss.

The marketing director's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes that all gym members share the same weight-loss goals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that members who are already more motivated to lose weight are also more likely to use the app.

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on a sample of gym members that may be too small to be reliable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats using the app as though it were the same thing as attending the gym regularly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that the gym offers several different membership tiers.

items.explanation: The director infers that app use causes weight loss purely from a correlation, without ruling out that motivation is a common cause of both app use and weight loss. B names exactly this failure to exclude a confounding variable, so it is correct. A raises an unrelated point about differing goals that the argument doesn't depend on. C alleges a sampling-size problem that the stimulus never raises. D wrongly conflates app use with gym attendance, a distinction the argument doesn't rely on. E is entirely irrelevant to the causal claim about weight loss.

items.stem:
Students who take a particular art elective score higher, on average, on standardized math tests than students who do not take the elective. A researcher concludes that taking the art elective improves students' math skills.

The researcher's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: fails to consider that students who choose to take the art elective might already be stronger students overall, for reasons unrelated to the elective.

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from the results at a single school to all schools nationwide.

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes that the standardized math tests accurately measure students' mathematical ability.

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that the art elective and the math test cover exactly the same skills.

choices.label: E
choices.text: dismisses the study's findings merely because they were funded by an arts organization.

items.explanation: The researcher concludes that the elective improves math skills merely because elective-takers score higher, without ruling out that stronger students self-select into the elective. A states this precisely, naming the failure to exclude a preexisting-ability confound, so it is correct. B alleges an unwarranted generalization to other schools that the stimulus never makes. C challenges test validity, a point the argument's causal inference doesn't depend on. D wrongly claims the argument assumes overlapping content between the elective and the test. E accuses the argument of a funding-based dismissal that never occurs in the stimulus.

items.stem: Principle: A city ordinance permits construction noise exceeding the standard decibel limit on residential streets only if (1) the work is an emergency repair necessary to prevent imminent harm to persons or property, and (2) the work is completed within twenty-four hours of when it began. Which of the following situations conforms to this principle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A utility crew works through the night to stop an active gas leak posing imminent danger to nearby homes, but the repair is not completed until thirty hours after it began.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A contractor performs a routine kitchen renovation, unrelated to any emergency, and finishes all the noisy work within twenty hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A tree service removes a large branch that shows no signs of imminent failure, purely as a precaution, completing the job in ten hours.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A plumbing crew repairs a burst water main that is actively flooding a home's basement, completing the emergency repair within eighteen hours of starting.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An emergency crew repairs a retaining wall that is on the verge of collapsing onto an adjacent house, but the noisy work is spread out intermittently over three days while the crew waits between inspection phases.

items.explanation: The principle demands both an imminent-harm emergency AND completion within twenty-four hours. D satisfies both: a flooding basement is imminent harm to property, and the repair wrapped up in eighteen hours -- this is the credited answer. A meets condition (1) (a gas leak is imminent harm) but fails condition (2): thirty hours exceeds the twenty-four-hour limit. B fails condition (1): a routine renovation is not an emergency repair, so the twenty-hour completion time is irrelevant. C fails condition (1): removing a branch with no sign of imminent failure is precautionary, not a response to imminent harm. E meets condition (1) (a collapsing wall threatens a house) but fails condition (2): the work stretches over three days, well past twenty-four hours.

items.stem: Principle: A university's tuition-refund policy grants a full refund for a withdrawn course only if (1) the student withdraws no later than the tenth day of the term, and (2) the student submits written notice of the withdrawal to the registrar's office. Which of the following situations conforms to this principle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A student decides to withdraw on the fifteenth day of the term and submits written notice to the registrar's office that same day.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A student decides to withdraw on the eighth day of the term and tells her professor about the decision in person, but never contacts the registrar's office.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A student decides to withdraw on the eighth day of the term and has a friend verbally inform the registrar's front-desk staff on his behalf.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A student decides on the fifth day of the term to withdraw but does not submit written notice to the registrar's office until the twelfth day.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A student decides to withdraw on the ninth day of the term and, that same day, emails written notice of the withdrawal to the registrar's office.

items.explanation: The principle requires both that withdrawal notice be given no later than the tenth day AND that the notice be written and directed to the registrar's office. E satisfies both: the notice was submitted on the ninth day, in writing, to the registrar -- this is the credited answer. A fails condition (1): the fifteenth day is past the tenth-day deadline, even though the notice was written and properly directed. B fails condition (2): telling a professor verbally is neither written nor sent to the registrar's office. C fails condition (2): a verbal message relayed by a friend is not written notice from the student. D fails condition (1): although the student decided to withdraw on the fifth day, the operative written notice was not submitted to the registrar until the twelfth day, past the deadline.

items.stem: Even though newly planted trees take five to ten years to generate significant shade, the city should nonetheless expand its street-tree planting program this year rather than wait for a less expensive option. Because sidewalk temperatures in unshaded neighborhoods now regularly exceed those in shaded neighborhoods by fifteen degrees during summer heat waves, and because heat-related hospital visits are concentrated almost entirely in those unshaded neighborhoods, delaying the program would allow a known public-health hazard to continue unaddressed for years longer than necessary.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city should expand its street-tree planting program this year rather than wait for a less expensive option.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Newly planted trees take five to ten years to generate significant shade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sidewalk temperatures in unshaded neighborhoods exceed those in shaded neighborhoods by fifteen degrees during summer heat waves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heat-related hospital visits are concentrated almost entirely in unshaded neighborhoods.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cheaper alternatives to the current tree-planting program are unlikely to ever become available.

items.explanation: The conclusion sits in the first sentence, right after the concession about slow shade growth: the city should expand the program now rather than wait, which A paraphrases. B merely restates the concession the author grants before arguing anyway -- the opposite of the author's own claim. C and D report the two 'because'-marked premises about the temperature gap and hospital visits, offered as evidence for acting now, not as the claim being argued for. E overreaches: the stimulus says the city should not wait for a cheaper option this year, but it never claims cheaper options will never exist -- that stronger claim is an unsupported implication the argument does not make.

items.stem:
Whenever a corporate board approves a merger without first holding a shareholder vote, the merger becomes subject to judicial review. TechCorp's board approved its merger with Datasoft without holding a shareholder vote. Therefore, TechCorp's shareholders are entitled to file suit to block the merger's implementation.

Which one of the following, if assumed, allows the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whenever a merger is subject to judicial review, its shareholders are entitled to file suit to block the merger's implementation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Shareholders are entitled to file suit to block a merger's implementation only if the merger is subject to judicial review.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Datasoft's shareholders were not consulted about the merger before the board's vote.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A merger that is subject to judicial review is likely to result in shareholders filing suit to block its implementation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: TechCorp's board has approved mergers without shareholder votes on previous occasions.

items.explanation: The premises establish, by modus ponens, that TechCorp's merger is subject to judicial review (approving without a shareholder vote triggers review, and TechCorp did exactly that). To reach the conclusion that shareholders are entitled to file suit, the argument needs a conditional guaranteeing that review status leads to suit entitlement. A supplies exactly this bridge (review → suit entitlement), making the conclusion airtight. B reverses the needed conditional (suit entitlement → review), which cannot establish that TechCorp's shareholders — already known to be under a merger subject to review — are entitled to sue; that is a classic converse error. C introduces an unestablished, irrelevant fact about consultation that never connects review status to suit entitlement. D only claims review 'likely' results in suit entitlement, a hedge that leaves open the possibility the conclusion is false, so it cannot make the argument valid. E cites TechCorp's past behavior, which has no bearing on whether this merger's review status entitles shareholders to sue now.

items.stem:
Nutritionist: Increasing dietary fiber intake reduces the risk of heart disease. In a yearlong study, participants who raised their daily fiber intake by at least 10 grams showed significantly lower cholesterol levels at the study's end than they had at its start.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the nutritionist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fiber supplements are inexpensive and widely available in grocery stores.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many participants found it difficult to maintain a high-fiber diet after the study ended.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lower cholesterol levels are strongly associated with reduced risk of heart disease.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The same participants also significantly increased their level of physical exercise during the year of the study.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fiber has been recommended by nutrition guidelines for over thirty years.

items.explanation: The nutritionist infers that fiber intake caused lower cholesterol merely because participants who raised fiber intake also saw cholesterol drop over the same year -- a correlation treated as causation. D supplies a concurrent alternate cause: increased exercise, which independently lowers cholesterol, so the observed drop cannot be confidently attributed to fiber alone; this directly severs the premise-to-conclusion link. A discusses cost, irrelevant to whether fiber caused the change. B addresses difficulty maintaining the diet after the study, which does not undermine what happened during the study itself. C actually supports the argument's assumed link between cholesterol and heart disease rather than attacking the fiber-to-cholesterol connection. E cites longstanding recommendations, which speaks to popularity, not causal efficacy.

items.stem:
Neighborhoods with more streetlights have lower rates of nighttime crime than neighborhoods with fewer streetlights. A city council member concludes that installing more streetlights reduces nighttime crime.

The council member's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: attacks the motives of officials who oppose the streetlight proposal rather than addressing their arguments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes that all neighborhoods have identical crime rates before any streetlights are installed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: uses the term "crime" to mean different things in different parts of the argument.

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to rule out the possibility that wealthier neighborhoods fund both streetlights and other crime-reducing measures, such as private security.

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes that installing streetlights is the only way the city could reduce nighttime crime.

items.explanation: The council member treats a correlation between streetlights and lower crime as proof of causation, without ruling out other explanations for the pattern. D supplies exactly such an alternative cause — wealth that funds both streetlights and private security — so it is correct. A alleges an ad hominem attack that is never made in the argument. B assumes a false premise about identical starting crime rates that the argument doesn't rely on. C alleges equivocation on "crime," but the term is used consistently throughout. E misstates the conclusion as an exclusivity claim, which was never asserted.

items.stem:
Towns that built new public libraries in the past decade have seen higher rates of small-business growth than towns that did not build new libraries. A regional economist concludes that building a public library spurs small-business growth.

The economist's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on business-growth figures that were self-reported by town officials.

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats "small-business growth" and "economic growth" as though they were the same thing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: dismisses, without argument, the experience of towns that did not build libraries.

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that every town in the region has roughly the same population size.

choices.label: E
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that towns already growing economically for independent reasons, such as new highway access, are simply better able to fund new libraries.

items.explanation: The economist infers that libraries spur business growth from a mere correlation, without ruling out that towns growing for independent reasons are simply better able to afford new libraries — a reverse-causation/common-cause possibility. E names this alternative cause, so it is correct. A raises a data-reliability worry that the stimulus never raises. B alleges a spurious equivocation; the argument keeps the two terms distinct. C mischaracterizes the argument as dismissing non-library towns, which it does not do. D assumes an irrelevant population-size premise that the argument doesn't require.

items.stem: Principle: A company's remote-work policy allows an employee to work from home on a given day only if (1) the employee's manager approves the request at least twenty-four hours in advance, and (2) the employee has no client-facing meetings scheduled for that day. Which of the following situations conforms to this principle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: On Wednesday morning, an employee requests to work from home the following Friday. The manager approves the request that same Wednesday, and Friday's calendar shows no client-facing meetings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An employee asks to work from home the morning of that same day, and the manager immediately approves the request. The employee has no client-facing meetings scheduled.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An employee requests to work from home three days in advance and receives the manager's approval, but the employee has a client call scheduled for that afternoon.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An employee sends the manager a message forty-eight hours in advance simply announcing that she will work from home that day. The manager never responds, and the employee has no client-facing meetings scheduled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An employee requests and receives the manager's approval a week in advance for a day with no meetings on the calendar. The day before, however, a colleague adds a client-facing meeting to the employee's calendar for that day.

items.explanation: The principle requires both manager approval given at least twenty-four hours ahead AND an empty client-facing schedule for that day. A satisfies both: approval came more than twenty-four hours before Friday, and no client meetings appear on the calendar -- this is the credited answer. B fails condition (1): approval was given the same morning, not twenty-four hours in advance. C meets condition (1) but fails condition (2): a client call is scheduled for that afternoon. D fails condition (1): announcing a plan is not the same as obtaining the manager's approval, and none was given. E met both conditions when approval was granted, but fails condition (2) as of the actual day: a client-facing meeting now appears on the calendar for that day.

items.stem:
Every certified arborist inspects a tree before recommending its removal. No certified arborist recommends removing a tree that is still fruit-bearing. The oak on Maple Avenue is still fruit-bearing.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The oak on Maple Avenue will never be removed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any tree that is not fruit-bearing will be recommended for removal by a certified arborist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A certified arborist has already inspected the oak on Maple Avenue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No certified arborist will recommend removing the oak on Maple Avenue.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If the oak on Maple Avenue stops bearing fruit, a certified arborist will recommend its removal.

items.explanation: D is correct: the second statement is a universal claim that no certified arborist recommends removing a fruit-bearing tree, and the third statement establishes that the oak is fruit-bearing, so the conclusion follows by direct instantiation of the rule. A overreaches -- the stimulus only limits what certified arborists will recommend, not whether the tree could be removed by any other means. B treats 'fruit-bearing, therefore not recommended' as if it also meant 'not fruit-bearing, therefore recommended,' an illicit converse. C misuses the first statement: inspection is a precondition for recommending removal, but since no removal will be recommended for this tree, no inspection is required to have occurred. E again treats the fruit-bearing condition as both necessary and sufficient for a recommendation, which the stimulus never establishes.

items.stem:
A software update may be deployed to production servers only if it has passed the automated regression suite. Version 4.2 of the billing module was deployed to production servers this morning. Therefore, version 4.2 of the billing module will not cause a customer-facing billing error this month.

Which one of the following, if assumed, allows the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An update that passes the automated regression suite is unlikely to cause a customer-facing billing error.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only updates that have been peer-reviewed by two engineers may be deployed to production servers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A software update does not cause a customer-facing billing error only if it has passed the automated regression suite.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Customers who report billing errors receive automatic refunds within forty-eight hours.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any software update that passes the automated regression suite will not cause a customer-facing billing error during the month it is deployed.

items.explanation: The 'only if' rule plus the fact that version 4.2 was deployed lets us conclude, by modus ponens, that it passed the automated regression suite. To reach the conclusion that it will cause no customer-facing billing errors this month, the argument needs a conditional guaranteeing that passing the suite rules out such errors. E supplies exactly this bridge (passed suite → no billing errors), making the conclusion airtight. A only claims such errors are 'unlikely,' a hedge that leaves room for the conclusion to be false. B introduces an unrelated deployment requirement (peer review) that never connects passing the suite to the absence of billing errors. C reverses the needed relationship (no billing errors → passed the suite), a converse error that cannot establish this update will avoid errors. D's fact about refund policy has no bearing on whether the update itself causes billing errors.

items.stem:
A pesticide may be approved for agricultural use only if it has undergone a decade-long toxicity study. This year, the Agriculture Ministry approved the pesticide Zorvex for agricultural use. Therefore, Zorvex will not accumulate in groundwater supplies near farmland where it is applied.

Which one of the following, if assumed, allows the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A pesticide that has undergone a decade-long toxicity study is somewhat less likely to accumulate in groundwater supplies near treated farmland.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any pesticide that has undergone a decade-long toxicity study will not accumulate in groundwater supplies near farmland where it is applied.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A pesticide does not accumulate in groundwater supplies near treated farmland only if it has undergone a decade-long toxicity study.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Farmers who apply Zorvex to their fields must wear protective equipment during application.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Zorvex has already been approved for agricultural use in several neighboring countries.

items.explanation: Because approval requires the decade-long toxicity study, and Zorvex was approved this year, modus ponens establishes that it underwent the study. The conclusion — that Zorvex will not accumulate in groundwater near treated farmland — requires a further conditional linking the study to that outcome. B supplies exactly this bridge (underwent study → no groundwater accumulation), guaranteeing the conclusion. A only claims accumulation is 'somewhat less likely,' a hedge that cannot rule out accumulation. C reverses the needed relationship (no accumulation → underwent study), a converse error that cannot show this already-studied pesticide will not accumulate. D introduces an unrelated safety requirement (protective equipment) that never connects the study to groundwater outcomes. E's fact about foreign approvals has no bearing on whether Zorvex accumulates in groundwater near farmland where it is applied.

items.stem:
Nutritionist: Last year, Acme Corp replaced its cafeteria's standard menu with nutritionist-designed, low-sugar meals. This year, the number of employee sick days taken company-wide fell by 18 percent compared to last year. The new menu must be responsible for the drop in sick days.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the nutritionist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cafeteria's new menu costs the company more per meal than the old menu did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The composition of Acme's workforce — age, department, and health history — was nearly identical in the two years compared.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several employees said they enjoy the taste of the new menu more than the old one.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A well-known nutrition expert has publicly praised menus similar to Acme's new one.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The same year the menu changed, Acme also let employees with minor illnesses work from home instead of taking a sick day.

items.explanation: The argument infers that the menu caused fewer sick days from a mere before-and-after correlation. B strengthens it by ruling out a key alternative explanation: that the drop reflects a change in who makes up the workforce (e.g., a shift toward employees already less prone to illness) rather than any effect of the menu. With the population held constant, the menu becomes the more plausible cause. A raises cost, which bears on expense, not on whether the menu improved health. C shows enjoyment of taste, which says nothing about whether health, and thus sick days, actually improved. D is an appeal to authority — an expert's praise doesn't show the menu caused this particular drop. E actually undermines the argument: if mildly ill employees now work from home instead of calling in sick, the metric could fall for administrative reasons unrelated to any real health improvement, so E is a weakener, not a strengthener.

items.stem:
School administrator: Since our district adopted the Read-25 program, which requires all elementary students to read silently for 25 minutes each morning, districtwide standardized reading scores have risen by 12 percent over the past two years. The Read-25 program must be responsible for this improvement.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the administrator's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Read-25 program cost the district less to implement than administrators had originally budgeted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prominent education researcher has publicly praised programs similar to Read-25.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reading scores in neighboring districts that did not adopt Read-25 remained flat over the same two years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The standardized reading test given this year was calibrated to be somewhat easier than the version given two years ago.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many parents have reported that their children enjoy the daily reading time.

items.explanation: The administrator infers causation from a two-year rise in scores that coincided with adopting Read-25. C strengthens the inference by supplying an implicit control group: comparable districts that did not adopt the program saw no such rise, which rules out a shared external cause — such as a statewide curriculum shift or a general trend — and isolates Read-25 as the likely factor. A speaks to budget, not to whether the program raised scores. B is an appeal to authority: praise for similar programs doesn't establish that Read-25 caused this district's gain. D actually weakens the argument, since an easier test could account for higher scores with no real improvement in reading ability. E reports satisfaction, not achievement, and so is irrelevant to whether scores rose because of the program.

items.stem:
Public safety official: Since the city installed brighter LED streetlights along Main Avenue last year, nighttime pedestrian accidents on that stretch have dropped by 30 percent. The brighter lighting must be responsible for the decline.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the official's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Traffic volume and posted speed limits along Main Avenue have not changed since the new lights were installed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The new LED streetlights consume less electricity than the sodium-vapor lights they replaced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A city council member with an engineering background voted in favor of the lighting upgrade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city also lowered the speed limit on Main Avenue by 10 miles per hour when the new lights were installed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The city plans to install similar LED lighting in three other neighborhoods next year.

items.explanation: The official attributes a drop in accidents to the new lighting based on a before-and-after comparison. A strengthens this by ruling out the two most obvious alternative causes of fewer accidents — reduced traffic and lower speed limits — leaving the lighting change as the more likely explanation for the decline. B addresses energy efficiency, which has no bearing on accident rates. C is an appeal to authority: a council member's engineering background doesn't show the lighting caused the drop. D actually weakens the argument by introducing exactly the kind of confound A rules out — a lowered speed limit that could itself explain fewer accidents. E concerns future plans elsewhere and says nothing about what caused the change already observed on Main Avenue.

items.stem:
Store manager: Our flagship store switched to new self-checkout software last spring, and average checkout wait times at that store fell by 40 percent over the following six months. Clearly, installing the new software caused the drop in wait times.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the manager's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The self-checkout software received a favorable review in a widely read technology trade magazine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The store also hired six additional cashiers to staff traditional checkout lanes during the same six-month period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Customers who used the new self-checkout kiosks reported that they were easy to operate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Installing the new software cost the store more than the previous checkout system had.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The store's total daily customer volume increased by 15 percent over the same six months.

items.explanation: The manager attributes the drop in wait times solely to the new software based on the timing of the installation coinciding with the improvement. B supplies a concurrent alternate cause -- additional cashier staffing -- that could account for shorter average wait times independent of the software, undermining the causal claim. A cites a magazine review, which speaks to reputation, not to what actually caused wait times to fall. C reports user satisfaction with ease of use, which does not establish that the software rather than something else reduced overall wait times. D raises installation cost, an irrelevant consideration. E, if anything, makes the software's apparent effect more impressive since wait times fell despite more customers, so it does not weaken and may even bolster the conclusion.

items.stem:
Orchard owner: We introduced ladybugs into the orchard to control the aphid population. Aphid counts, which had been rising for months, fell sharply within three weeks of the release. Clearly, introducing the ladybugs caused the decline in aphids.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the orchard owner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The three-week period in which aphid counts fell coincided with an unusually cold snap known to sharply reduce aphid reproduction rates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ladybugs are commonly used by orchard owners across the region to manage pest populations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Purchasing and releasing the ladybugs cost the orchard less than a comparable application of pesticide would have.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aphids are a significant threat to fruit tree yields if left unchecked.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some of the released ladybugs migrated to a neighboring farm within a month of the release.

items.explanation: The owner infers that releasing ladybugs caused the aphid decline merely because the decline followed the release -- a temporal correlation, not proof of causation. A supplies a concurrent alternate cause: an unusually cold period known to independently suppress aphid reproduction, which could fully explain the drop without any effect from the ladybugs, undermining the causal claim. B cites the popularity of the ladybug method elsewhere, irrelevant to what happened in this orchard. C addresses cost, not causation. D restates why aphid control matters generally, not why the ladybugs specifically caused this decline. E's detail about later migration does not address what caused the decline that had already occurred within the first three weeks.

items.stem:
Public health official: Since our city began requiring restaurants to post calorie counts on menus five years ago, the citywide obesity rate has fallen by three percentage points. Clearly, then, mandatory calorie labeling has caused the decline in the obesity rate.

The public health official's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: presupposes what it sets out to prove.

choices.label: B
choices.text: takes for granted that no factor other than calorie labeling could account for the decline in the obesity rate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the whole city from evidence concerning only a few restaurants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats a condition that is sufficient to reduce obesity as though it were also necessary to reduce it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejects the effectiveness of calorie labeling merely because some restaurants have not complied with it.

items.explanation: The official infers causation from mere temporal correlation: the labeling requirement preceded the decline, so it is credited as the cause, without ruling out other explanations (broader health campaigns, economic shifts, changing food trends). That is exactly what B names. A is wrong because the argument never assumes its conclusion as a premise; it offers a flawed causal inference, not circular reasoning. C is wrong because the argument cites a citywide statistic, not a restaurant subsample, so there is no part-to-whole generalization. D is wrong because the argument never claims labeling is required for obesity to decline; it claims labeling caused the decline, which is a different error. E is wrong because the passage never discusses noncompliance or rejects anything on that basis.

items.stem:
Librarian: This year, mystery novels were checked out more times than books from any other single genre in our collection. Clearly, mystery is our patrons' favorite genre. Since a public library's acquisitions budget should track what its patrons love most, the mystery collection should receive the largest share of next year's acquisitions budget.

The librarian's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on checkout data from a single year to draw a conclusion about patrons' preferences over time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: equates the frequency with which mystery novels are checked out with how highly patrons regard the mystery genre relative to others, though frequent checkouts may simply reflect that mystery novels are quick reads that get returned and reborrowed often.

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes, without justification, that patrons who check out mystery novels never also check out books from other genres.

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats a proposed budget policy as though it had already been adopted and implemented.

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that some patrons acquire mystery novels by purchasing them rather than borrowing them from the library.

items.explanation: The librarian moves from checkout frequency (how often mystery novels leave the shelves) to patron preference (how much patrons value the genre above others), treating the two as the same thing. A genre can top the checkout count simply because its books are short and get returned and reborrowed quickly, not because patrons prize it most; B names this shift. A alleges a hasty generalization from one year of data, but the conclusion concerns next year's budget given this year's demonstrated demand, not a claim about long-term preference stability, so A misdescribes the argument. C invents an unstated and irrelevant assumption about exclusive borrowing habits that the argument never needs. D is inapplicable because the librarian only recommends a budget allocation and never treats it as already enacted. E raises purchasing habits, a consideration outside the scope of an argument built entirely on library checkout data.

items.stem:
Urban planner: The city council's new zoning law requires that fifteen percent of units in any large residential development be designated "affordable housing."
