Developers have complied by pricing those units at just below the citywide median sale price. Because compliance with the law has been high, the zoning law is succeeding at making housing affordable for low-income residents.

The urban planner's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes that every developer subject to the zoning law has complied with it in good faith.

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a correlation between the zoning law's passage and current housing prices as evidence that the law caused those prices.

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the citywide housing market from the pricing practices of only a few developments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: equates housing priced just below the citywide median sale price with housing that is genuinely within reach of low-income residents, even though the median sale price may still be far higher than what such residents can afford.

choices.label: E
choices.text: assumes that low-income residents prefer to live in large residential developments rather than in smaller buildings.

items.explanation: The planner treats "affordable housing" in its technical, regulatory sense (priced just below the citywide median) as equivalent to housing that is actually affordable for low-income residents, though a price just under the citywide median can still be well beyond a low-income budget. D names this shift. A is inapplicable because compliance is stated as a given fact, not an assumption the argument needs to be true in good faith. B is wrong because the argument never claims the law caused housing prices generally, only that compliant units were priced a certain way. C mischaracterizes the premise, which describes developers broadly, not "only a few" developments. E is irrelevant: preferences about building size have no bearing on whether the mandated units are financially reachable.

items.stem: In Meadowbrook County, farmers planted a record-high proportion of a new drought-resistant corn hybrid this year—a hybrid documented to outyield standard corn under moderately dry conditions. Yet the county's total corn yield this year was lower than last year's, when farmers planted almost none of the new hybrid. Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain this apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: This year's growing season brought rainfall levels far below normal—well beyond the moderate dryness the hybrid was bred to tolerate—so the hybrid's yield advantage was overwhelmed by the severity of the drought.

choices.label: B
choices.text: National corn prices fell by double digits this year compared to last year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The record planting of the drought-resistant hybrid was concentrated on the county's largest farms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drought-resistant hybrid tends to produce its highest yields specifically in years of severe, rather than moderate, drought.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Last year's corn crop, but not this year's, was afflicted by a fungal blight that has since been eradicated.

items.explanation: The paradox: record planting of a hybrid known to outyield standard corn under dry conditions, yet total yield fell. (A) resolves it by showing the hybrid's documented advantage applies only to moderate dryness—this year's drought exceeded that threshold, so even the superior hybrid could not prevent an overall decline; both facts hold simultaneously. (B) is out of scope: price movements don't explain yield. (C) only describes where planting occurred, not why total yield fell; it doesn't address the discrepancy. (D) deepens the paradox—if severe drought is exactly when the hybrid performs best, the yield drop becomes even harder to explain. (E) also deepens the paradox: removing a disease that suppressed last year's yield should have made this year's yield relatively higher, not lower, making the actual decline more puzzling, not less.

items.stem: In Silverwood National Park, the gray wolf population has more than doubled over the past decade due to a successful reintroduction program. Yet the population of elk, the wolves' primary prey, has not declined over that same period—it has remained essentially stable. Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain this apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The park's wolves hunt in coordinated packs, which increases their hunting success rate compared to solitary wolves.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Silverwood's wolves prey primarily on elk that are old, sick, or injured—individuals that generally would not have survived long or reproduced successfully regardless, so increased predation has mainly removed elk that contributed little to future population growth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elk are herbivores that feed primarily on the grasses and shrubs found throughout the park's meadows.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A separate elk population in a neighboring, wolf-free preserve has grown substantially over the past decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The reintroduction program initially released only a small number of breeding pairs of wolves a decade ago.

items.explanation: The paradox: the wolf population more than doubled, yet elk numbers held steady. (B) resolves it by showing predation has concentrated on elk unlikely to have added to the population anyway, so the rise in wolf numbers hasn't translated into a corresponding loss of reproductively significant elk—both facts can be true together. (A) deepens the paradox: a higher hunting success rate should mean more elk killed and a declining population, making the observed stability harder to explain. (C) is out of scope: elk diet says nothing about predation's effect on their population. (D) is out of scope: a wolf-free preserve is a separate population and cannot explain trends within Silverwood itself. (E) explains only how the wolf population grew from a small founding group, not why elk numbers failed to fall in response.

items.stem:
City council member: Two years ago, Midvale launched a curbside composting program, and the city's landfill waste dropped by 30 percent within a year. Because Elmwood resembles Midvale in population size and household density, launching a curbside composting program in Elmwood will likewise reduce its landfill waste by about 30 percent.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the council member's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Composting bins are inexpensive to manufacture and distribute.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Midvale residents widely praised the composting program in a satisfaction survey.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elmwood's landfill waste has increased slightly over the past several years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several other cities besides Midvale have also successfully reduced landfill waste through composting programs.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unlike Midvale, Elmwood does not have municipal trucks equipped to separately collect compostable waste, and outfitting them would take several years.

items.explanation: The council member reasons by analogy: because Elmwood resembles Midvale in population and density, a composting program should produce a similar result there. E identifies a relevant disanalogy -- Elmwood lacks the collection infrastructure that made Midvale's program work and cannot quickly acquire it -- which severs the inference that demographic similarity implies similarity in outcome. A and B raise cost and popularity in Midvale, neither of which bears on whether Elmwood's program would succeed. C's preexisting waste trend in Elmwood does not address the comparison to Midvale's causal result one way or the other. D actually adds more supporting analogues rather than weakening the argument. Only E attacks the premise-to-conclusion link directly.

items.stem:
Analyst: After installing new machinery last year, our factory used twelve percent less energy to produce the same volume of goods as the year before. Since efficiency is simply a matter of using fewer resources to achieve the same output, the new machinery made the factory more efficient. It follows that operating the factory cost less last year than it did the year before.

The analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers that the decrease in energy use was caused by the new machinery, without ruling out that the factory simply produced a smaller volume of goods last year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a twelve percent decrease in energy use as though it were a decrease of twelve absolute units of energy, rather than a percentage of a larger total.

choices.label: C
choices.text: concludes that the factory's overall profits increased without providing any data about the factory's revenue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the factory's future operating costs based on a single year of data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: equates using fewer resources to produce a given output with spending less money to operate the factory, even though resource efficiency and total operating cost can diverge because of factors such as energy prices, maintenance, and labor.

items.explanation: The analyst equates technical efficiency (fewer resources per unit of output) with financial cost (money spent to operate the factory), but these can diverge: energy prices, maintenance needs, or labor costs could rise even as resource efficiency improves. E names this measure shift. A is contradicted by the stimulus, which states output volume held constant, so the alternative it proposes cannot explain the data. B alleges a numerical misreading the analyst never makes; the argument treats the percentage correctly as a proportional decrease. C is out of scope because the analyst concludes only that operating cost fell, never mentioning profit or revenue. D mischaracterizes the conclusion, which is a claim about last year's cost compared to the prior year, not a prediction about future years.

items.stem: After a hospital introduced a new hand-hygiene training program, the proportion of staff observed washing their hands according to protocol rose from 62 percent to 91 percent. Yet the hospital's overall rate of hospital-acquired infections was no lower in the year after the program than in the year before. Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain this apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The hospital's patient satisfaction survey scores improved after the training program was introduced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Studies of similar programs at other hospitals have found that compliance rates typically decline within a year unless reinforced by ongoing training.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nurses who attended the training reported that they found the hand-washing techniques easy to remember and apply.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The hospital also introduced a new antibiotic protocol during the same year, one shown at other facilities to reduce post-procedure infection rates by roughly 30 percent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: During that year, the hospital began admitting significantly more patients transferred from a nearby long-term-care facility that closed, and these patients had unusually weakened immune systems that made them more susceptible to infection independent of hand hygiene.

items.explanation: The paradox: measured hand-hygiene compliance rose dramatically, yet the infection rate didn't budge. (E) resolves it by identifying a shift in the patient population toward individuals far more vulnerable to infection for reasons unrelated to hygiene—so improved hand-washing could be genuinely reducing hygiene-related transmission while a sicker patient mix pushed the overall rate back up, letting both facts hold. (A) is out of scope: satisfaction scores don't bear on infection rates. (B) is a generalization about other hospitals' future compliance trends, not a fact about what actually happened at this hospital during the year in question, so it doesn't address the current discrepancy. (C) explains only why compliance rose (staff found the training memorable), saying nothing about the infection rate. (D) deepens the paradox: an additional intervention independently expected to lower infections should have made the flat rate even more surprising, not less.

items.stem:
Marine biologists agree that a coral reef's ability to survive a period of unusually warm ocean water depends heavily on the reef's genetic diversity: greater diversity gives a reef's coral colonies more chances of carrying heat-tolerant gene variants. Of all the reefs in the Coral Strait region, Kestrel Reef has the greatest genetic diversity. Marine biologists therefore predict that, of the region's reefs, Kestrel Reef is the one most likely to survive the coming period of unusually warm water.

Which one of the following is an assumption required by the marine biologists' prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Kestrel Reef's genetic diversity arose primarily through natural processes rather than human intervention.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genetic diversity is the only factor that affects a coral reef's ability to survive warm water.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kestrel Reef will receive priority protection from regional conservation authorities because of its genetic diversity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No other reef in the Coral Strait region has some other advantage relevant to surviving warm water great enough to offset Kestrel Reef's lead in genetic diversity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every coral colony within Kestrel Reef carries at least one heat-tolerant gene variant.

items.explanation: The prediction moves from 'Kestrel has the most genetic diversity' to 'Kestrel is most likely to survive,' which only follows if nothing else could tip the balance toward a different reef. D supplies exactly that: negate it - suppose some other reef DOES have an offsetting advantage - and Kestrel's diversity lead no longer makes it the likeliest survivor, so the prediction fails; D is required. A is out of scope: how the diversity arose doesn't bear on survival odds. B overshoots what's needed - the argument only requires that no other factor overcome Kestrel's edge, not that diversity is the sole relevant factor, so B is stronger than necessary. C is irrelevant: conservation funding doesn't affect biological survival likelihood. E misreads the premise, which says diversity gives 'more chances that some colonies' carry heat-tolerant genes, not that every colony does; E is an unwarranted overstatement the argument never needs.

items.stem:
Swim coach: Since our team started reviewing weekly underwater video of each athlete's stroke technique, athletes' race times have improved by an average of 3 percent this season. The video review sessions must be responsible for the improvement.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the coach's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The underwater cameras used for video review were relatively inexpensive compared to other training equipment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An Olympic swimming coach has recommended video review as a training tool.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The team also hired a new strength-and-conditioning coach at the start of this season.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Athletes who received the most correction feedback during video sessions improved their times the most, while athletes who received little feedback improved the least.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several athletes said that watching themselves swim on video was initially embarrassing.

items.explanation: The coach infers that video review caused the season's improvement from a general correlation between the new practice and faster times. D strengthens the argument by confirming the underlying mechanism: within the team, the amount of feedback an athlete received tracks the size of that athlete's improvement, a dose-response pattern that is hard to explain unless the video review itself is driving the gains. A concerns cost, not effectiveness. B is an appeal to authority — a coach's endorsement doesn't demonstrate that video review caused this team's improvement. C actually weakens the argument by introducing a rival explanation, the new strength-and-conditioning coach, for the same improvement. E describes athletes' discomfort, which is irrelevant to whether the sessions improved performance.

items.stem:
Manager: To qualify for the senior analyst role at our firm, an employee must complete the advanced certification course. Priya has completed the advanced certification course. So Priya will be promoted to senior analyst.

The manager's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers that Priya lacks any additional qualifications, since none were mentioned.

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats the fact that the course does not guarantee promotion as proof that the course is irrelevant to promotion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from a single employee's situation to a conclusion about every employee at the firm.

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats a condition required for the promotion as though it were, by itself, enough to secure the promotion.

choices.label: E
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that the certification requirement has changed since Priya completed the course.

items.explanation: The stated rule makes completing the course a necessary condition for promotion, not a sufficient one. From the fact that Priya satisfied that necessary condition, the manager concludes she will be promoted, illegitimately treating the requirement as though meeting it alone guarantees the outcome. That is D. A is wrong: the argument never addresses (nor denies) Priya's other qualifications, so this criticism has no textual basis. B is wrong: the manager never claims the course is worthless or irrelevant; that is the reverse of the actual error. C is wrong: the conclusion concerns only Priya, not a firm-wide claim about every employee. E is wrong: nothing in the passage suggests the requirement changed; this introduces an unsupported possibility.

items.stem:
Coach: This season, our team's average points scored per game increased by ten points over last season's average. Our team's performance has therefore improved this season. Since a team is nothing more than the sum of its individual players, every player on this year's roster must have improved compared to last season.

The coach's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats an increase in the team's aggregate scoring average as proof that each individual player's performance improved, without ruling out that the increase could instead result from personnel changes or a shift in playing time among returning players.

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that points scored per game is the only meaningful measure of a player's contribution to the team.

choices.label: C
choices.text: predicts that the team's scoring average will continue to rise in future seasons based on a single season's improvement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: dismisses evidence against the coach's conclusion by appealing to the players' popularity rather than to their statistics.

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that some opposing teams may have also increased their scoring averages this season.

items.explanation: "Improved" shifts from a team-level, aggregate sense (the average went up) to a distributive, individual sense (every single player got better), as if a team's total were nothing but a simple sum of unchanged parts. But the aggregate could rise because of new players, cut players, or redistributed playing time, with no single returning player improving at all; A names exactly this scope shift. B alleges an unstated assumption about points being the sole measure of contribution, which the coach's argument does not require. C mischaracterizes the conclusion, which is about last season versus this season, not future seasons. D is inapplicable since nothing in the passage appeals to popularity. E raises other teams' performance, which is irrelevant to whether this team's own players individually improved.

items.stem:
Every accredited clinic is inspected each year. Every clinic that is inspected each year keeps a public compliance log. Riverside is an accredited clinic. Therefore, Riverside keeps a public compliance log.

The pattern of reasoning above is most closely paralleled by which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most novels that win the prize are translated into English, and most translated novels sell well abroad. This novel won the prize, so it sells well abroad.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every bonded courier is fingerprinted, and every fingerprinted courier is assigned an ID number. Lopez has an ID number, so Lopez is a bonded courier.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every commissioned mural is catalogued, and every catalogued artwork is insured. The atrium piece is a commissioned mural, so the atrium piece is insured.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every scholarship recipient volunteers, and everyone who volunteers earns service credit. Nina is not a scholarship recipient, so Nina earns no service credit.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every registered drone is logged, and every logged drone is either taxed or exempted. This drone is registered, so it is taxed.

items.explanation: The stimulus chains two universals and instantiates: all P are Q; all Q are R; a is P; therefore a is R. C reproduces it exactly (mural to catalogued to insured, and the atrium piece is a mural, so it is insured). A downgrades both universals to 'most,' so the probabilistic links cannot chain to a certainty about a particular novel. B runs the chain backward, inferring membership from the end term (ID number)—affirming the consequent. D denies the antecedent, concluding from 'not P' that the consequent fails. E replaces the second universal's predicate with a disjunction (taxed or exempted), so 'taxed' cannot be guaranteed. Only C preserves both the validity and the forward P-to-R structure.

items.stem:
If a bill has broad support, it clears committee. If a bill clears committee, it reaches the floor for a vote. The reform bill never reached the floor for a vote. Therefore, the reform bill did not have broad support.

Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a resume is flagged, it goes to a recruiter. If it goes to a recruiter, it gets a phone screen. This resume got a phone screen, so it was flagged.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the river floods, the trail closes. If the trail closes, the race is postponed. The river did not flood, so the race was not postponed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a shrub is native, it needs little watering. Most shrubs that need little watering survive the summer. This shrub did not survive the summer, so it is not native.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a nominee is endorsed, she secures funding. If she gains media coverage, she wins her primary. She did not win her primary, so she was not endorsed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If the alarm is armed, the sensors are live. If the sensors are live, the log records any motion. The log recorded no motion overnight. So the alarm was not armed.

items.explanation: The stimulus chains two conditionals and applies modus tollens: P to Q; Q to R; not R; therefore not P. E reproduces it—armed to sensors live to log records motion; the log recorded none; so it was not armed. A affirms the consequent, inferring the antecedent (flagged) from the final result (phone screen). B denies the antecedent, moving from 'river did not flood' to 'race not postponed.' C downgrades the second link to 'most,' so the chain cannot deliver a valid contrapositive from 'did not survive.' D breaks the chain: the middle terms (secures funding vs. gains media coverage) do not connect, so 'not endorsed' does not follow from 'did not win.' Only E preserves the valid P-Q-R-then-deny-R form.

items.stem:
Analyst: If a company's quarterly earnings beat analyst forecasts, its share price rises the next trading day. Meridian Corp's share price rose the trading day after it released its quarterly report. It follows that Meridian's earnings beat the forecasts.

Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its flawed reasoning to the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a highway is salted before a storm, it stays free of ice. The county salted Route 9 before Tuesday's storm, so Route 9 stayed free of ice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a patient has completed the antibiotic course, the follow-up culture shows no bacterial growth. Ms. Alvarez's culture showed no growth, so she completed the course.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a seedling receives direct sun, it flowers early. This seedling gets no direct sun, so it will not flower early.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the smoke alarm is working, it sounds when the test button is held. The alarm did not sound when the button was held, so it is not working.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every tenant who pays rent late is sent a notice. Mr. Okafor paid his rent late this month, so he was sent a notice.

items.explanation: The analyst reasons: earnings-beat -> price rise; the price rose; therefore earnings beat. That affirms the consequent, since a price rise could have other causes. (B) matches exactly: completed course -> no growth; no growth observed; therefore completed course. (A) is a valid modus ponens (salted, so ice-free). (C) denies the antecedent (no sun, so no early flowering) -- invalid, but a different conditional error. (D) is a valid modus tollens (didn't sound, so not working). (E) is a valid universal instantiation (paid late, so sent a notice). Only (B) commits the analyst's affirm-the-consequent flaw.

items.stem:
Harbormaster: If the evening ferry is running, the harbor cafe stays open past nine. Tonight the evening ferry is not running. So the harbor cafe will not stay open past nine.

Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its flawed reasoning to the harbormaster's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a bill has bipartisan backing, it clears the committee. The transit bill cleared the committee, so it had bipartisan backing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the vaccine is effective, reported cases decline. Reported cases did not decline, so the vaccine is not effective.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a student submits the essay before Friday, she is entered in the prize draw. Devon did not submit his essay before Friday, so Devon is not entered in the draw.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the thermostat is set below sixty, the heater runs. The thermostat is set below sixty, so the heater is running.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every club member who renewed by June received a badge. Priya renewed by June, so Priya received a badge.

items.explanation: The harbormaster reasons: ferry running -> cafe open late; ferry not running; therefore cafe not open late. That denies the antecedent, since the cafe could stay open for other reasons. (C) matches: submits early -> entered; Devon didn't submit early; therefore not entered. (A) affirms the consequent (cleared committee, so bipartisan) -- invalid, but the opposite conditional error. (B) is a valid modus tollens (cases didn't decline, so not effective). (D) is a valid modus ponens (set below sixty, so running). (E) is a valid universal instantiation (renewed, so got a badge). Only (C) commits the deny-the-antecedent flaw.

items.stem: Over the past five years, ridership on Ridgeline Transit's commuter rail line grew by 40 percent. Yet automobile traffic congestion on the parallel highway during rush hour did not decrease at all over that same period. Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve this apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ridgeline Transit added several new rail cars during the five years to accommodate its growing ridership.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The rail line's ticket prices rose by 15 percent over the five years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The region's total commuter population grew by more than 60 percent over the same five years, so despite the rail line's growth, the number of commuters choosing to drive also increased substantially.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The parallel highway gained two additional lanes of capacity through a widening project completed during the five years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ridgeline Transit's on-time performance improved significantly over the five years.

items.explanation: The paradox: rail ridership rose sharply, yet highway congestion didn't ease at all. (C) resolves it: if the overall pool of commuters grew even faster than rail ridership, the rail line could be absorbing real new demand while the number of drivers still rose, holding congestion steady. (A) explains only how the transit agency accommodated more riders—it says nothing about why driving volume held up, so it addresses only one side of the paradox. (B) is out of scope: fare changes don't bear on congestion levels. (D) deepens the paradox: added highway capacity plus rising rail ridership should have eased congestion further, making its absence more surprising, not less. (E) is out of scope: better on-time performance might explain why riders chose the train, but it does not explain why car traffic failed to drop.

items.stem:
A city planner claims: "Every proposed park design that includes a water feature will exceed our maintenance budget, so we should reject any design with a water feature." A colleague responds: "That's not quite right. The Riverside plan includes a decorative fountain, yet its projected upkeep cost is the lowest of all twelve submitted designs — well under budget."

The colleague responds to the city planner's claim by

choices.label: A
choices.text: presenting a specific case that meets the stated condition but not the predicted outcome, thereby refuting the planner's generalization with a counterexample

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogous conclusion about a different budgeting decision and arguing that the same reasoning must apply there as well

choices.label: C
choices.text: showing that accepting the planner's claim would lead to a result that is self-contradictory or plainly absurd

choices.label: D
choices.text: citing the judgment of a budget expert whose credentials make that expert's opinion authoritative on the matter

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that the only two explanations for the fountain's low cost are the planner's assumption and mere coincidence, then eliminating coincidence

items.explanation: A is correct: the colleague identifies a case — the Riverside plan — that satisfies the planner's stated condition (includes a water feature) but not the predicted consequence (exceeding budget), which is precisely how a counterexample refutes a universal generalization. B is wrong because the colleague never reasons by analogy to a different budgeting decision; the response stays within the same set of designs. C is wrong because the colleague never claims the planner's view produces an absurd or self-contradictory result — only that it produces a false prediction. D is wrong because no expert's authority is invoked; the evidence offered is the Riverside plan's own projected costs, not anyone's opinion. E is wrong because the colleague does not present or eliminate rival explanations for the fountain's low cost; the point is simply that the planner's generalization has an exception.

A software company can win a lucrative government contract only if its product passes an independent security audit. The company's product has just passed an independent security audit conducted by GlobalCert, a security firm with an excellent reputation. The company's chief executive therefore announced that the company will win the government contract.

The chief executive's conclusion depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: GlobalCert's security audits are more rigorous than those conducted by other security-auditing firms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No requirement other than passing a security audit could prevent the company from winning the government contract.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The company has previously won government contracts on the strength of a security audit alone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a company's product fails an independent security audit, the government will not award that company the contract.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The government awards this particular contract to only one company each year.

items.explanation: Passing the audit is stated only as a necessary condition for winning ('can win only if'), so from 'passed the audit' alone nothing follows about actually winning unless nothing else stands in the way. B supplies that missing link; negate it - suppose some other requirement could still block the win - and the CEO's conclusion no longer follows, so B is required. A is out of scope: relative audit rigor doesn't establish that passing guarantees the contract. C is irrelevant history that doesn't bear on this contract. D merely restates the given 'only if' premise in its contrapositive form (failing the audit blocks the contract); it's already true given the premises and adds nothing to bridge from 'passed' to 'will win,' so it isn't the missing assumption. E introduces an unstated, unnecessary detail about how many companies are awarded the contract.

items.stem:
Community organizer: A sustainable neighborhood is one that can meet its own needs without depleting resources for future generations. Our neighborhood has sustained a stable population and tax base for over twenty years. Therefore, our neighborhood is a sustainable neighborhood.

The community organizer's reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it...

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes that a neighborhood's needs never change over a twenty-year period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: infers that because the neighborhood has been stable for twenty years, it will remain stable indefinitely.

choices.label: C
choices.text: trades on two different senses of "sustain," shifting from a neighborhood's staying stable over time to a neighborhood's not depleting resources for the future.

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the absence of any reported resource shortages as proof that the neighborhood does not deplete resources.

choices.label: E
choices.text: concludes that the neighborhood meets the stated definition merely because community members believe that it does.

items.explanation: The definition given uses "sustainable" to mean not depleting resources for the future, but the evidence offered concerns a different sense of the word: a stable population and tax base sustained over time. The argument treats satisfying this second, unrelated sense as though it satisfied the first, which is equivocation, named by C. A is wrong: the argument never claims needs are static; that issue is not raised. B is wrong: the conclusion is about the present, not a prediction of indefinite future stability. D is wrong: no resource shortages or reports are mentioned anywhere in the passage. E is wrong: the argument cites financial and demographic stability, not community members' beliefs, as its evidence.

items.stem:
Board member: The gallery's loss last quarter was caused either by falling attendance or by rising rent. Attendance did fall last quarter. So rising rent was not a factor in the loss.

Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its flawed reasoning to the board member's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The malfunction is in either the software or the hardware. Testing shows it is not in the software. So it is in the hardware.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The proposal is not both cheap and fast. It is certainly cheap. So it is not fast.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the gallery had cut its staff, its costs would have dropped. Its costs did drop. So the gallery cut its staff.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marcus was late this morning because he either overslept or missed his train. He did oversleep. So he did not miss his train.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If the loss came from rent, then rent rose this quarter. Rent did not rise. So the loss did not come from rent.

items.explanation: The board member treats an 'either/or' as exclusive: the loss came from falling attendance or rising rent; attendance fell; therefore rent was not a factor. But both causes could operate at once, so affirming one disjunct does not rule out the other. (D) commits the same error: overslept or missed the train; he overslept; so he didn't miss the train. (A) is a valid disjunctive syllogism (not software, so hardware). (B) is a valid De Morgan inference (not both cheap and fast; cheap; so not fast). (C) affirms the consequent (cut staff -> costs drop; costs dropped; so cut staff). (E) is a valid modus tollens (rent didn't rise, so the loss was not from rent). Only (D) affirms a disjunct.

An engineer argues: "Last month, the factory's defect rate fell sharply. Either the new quality-control checklist caused the drop, the milder weather reduced humidity-related warping, or the reassignment of the night-shift supervisor improved oversight. We can rule out the weather: temperature and humidity logs show conditions nearly identical to the prior month. We can also rule out the supervisor reassignment: the new supervisor wasn't scheduled to start until three weeks after the drop had already leveled off. So the checklist must be responsible."

The engineer's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: inferring that the checklist caused the drop merely because the two events happened to occur around the same time, without considering whether other factors might explain the timing

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing a general rule about defect rates from a single factory's experience and applying that rule to the manufacturing industry as a whole

choices.label: C
choices.text: presuming, without independent proof, that quality-control checklists are inherently effective, and using that presumption to account for the data

choices.label: D
choices.text: eliminating two competing explanations for the observed drop by citing independent evidence against each, leaving the remaining explanation as the best-supported one

choices.label: E
choices.text: comparing the factory's situation to an analogous case at a different plant where a checklist also coincided with a reduction in defects

items.explanation: D is correct: the engineer considers three candidate explanations, rules out two of them using independent evidence (matching weather logs; a supervisor start date after the drop had leveled off), and concludes that the surviving explanation is responsible — the classic method of eliminating alternatives. A is wrong because the engineer does not rely on mere timing; the argument explicitly rules out the two other candidates using evidence unrelated to timing, rather than inferring causation from correlation alone. B is wrong because no general industry-wide rule is drawn or applied; the conclusion is limited to this factory's defect rate. C is wrong because the engineer never simply presumes checklists work; the conclusion rests on ruling out rivals, not on an unproven assumption about checklists in general. E is wrong because no other plant or analogous case is mentioned anywhere in the argument.

items.stem:
Historians know that a town's founding date is best established by contemporaneous written records. The earliest surviving municipal document that mentions the town of Millbrook is dated 1841, and no surviving document assigns Millbrook an earlier founding date. Historians have therefore concluded that Millbrook was founded in 1841.

Which one of the following is an assumption required by the historians' reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Millbrook's 1841 municipal document is the oldest surviving document of its kind in the entire region.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most towns founded before 1841 have surviving records of their founding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Millbrook's municipal records from 1841 onward are completely accurate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Written records are the only reliable evidence of a town's founding date.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If Millbrook had been founded before 1841, some written record of that founding would have survived to the present.

items.explanation: The historians infer 'founded in 1841' from 'no surviving document says earlier,' which is an appeal to absent evidence. That inference holds only if an earlier founding would have left a surviving trace. Negate E - suppose Millbrook could have been founded earlier without any record surviving - and the absence of an earlier-dated document proves nothing, so E is required. A compares Millbrook's document to other regional documents, which is irrelevant to Millbrook's own founding date. B speaks only to a general statistical tendency across other towns and doesn't establish what would have happened in Millbrook's specific case, so it's the wrong scope to do the needed work. C concerns the accuracy of later records, not whether any record of an earlier founding would exist, so it's out of scope. D overshoots: the argument doesn't need written records to be the only reliable evidence in general, only that an earlier founding of Millbrook specifically would have produced a surviving one.
